Hook: In the 1940s, an American plant scientist named Norman Borlaug went to Mexico to help its farmers grow more wheat. The wheat they grew was tall and thin. Feed it fertilizer, and its heads grew heavy, and the stalks bent and fell over before harvest, flattening the crop into the mud. So Borlaug and his team bred a short wheat, a dwarf, with a thick stem that could carry a big head of grain without falling. They crossed thousands of plants, two crops a year, in two corners of the country. By 1956, Mexico grew all the wheat it needed. In the mid-1960s the dwarf wheat went to India and Pakistan, where famine was feared, and production rose enormously. In 1970 Borlaug won the Nobel Peace Prize, for having given, in the committee's words, a well-founded hope: the green revolution.

Here is what followed, in the data the United Nations' Food and Agriculture Organization has kept since 1961: tonnes of wheat harvested from each hectare. In the 1960s, India and Pakistan harvested less than a tonne a hectare. Watch them climb as the new wheat, fertilizer and irrigation spread. Since 1961 India's yield has multiplied 4.2 times, Pakistan's 4.0, Mexico's 3.4, and the world's 3.3. The famines that many experts predicted for the 1970s did not come on anything like the scale they feared. It is one of the greatest things any industry has ever done.

And yet. Take a dollar that an American spent on food in 2025, at a supermarket or a restaurant. According to the Department of Agriculture's economists, about 12.6 cents of it went to farms. The other 87-odd cents went to everything that happens after the farm gate: processing, packing, shipping, selling, cooking and serving. Farmers have multiplied what an acre can grow, again and again, and kept a small and shrinking slice of what we pay for food. This part is about why.
Industry, Built. Part ten: farming and food. Why do farmers grow ever more, and keep so little of what we pay?
Run: Chapter one. Run it: three seasons.

Play it yourself. You farm corn in Iowa, on about three hundred acres, the size of the typical corn farm in the Department of Agriculture's cost survey. Every spring you decide how much of the crop you expect to sell ahead, at today's price for delivery after harvest. That is called hedging, or forward selling. You can sell none of it, half, or all. And every autumn, whatever you have not already sold, you either sell at harvest or keep in a bin until the following June, hoping the price rises by more than the cost of storing it. You will play three real seasons, with the real yields, costs and prices of those years. You do not know which years they are. Pause, and choose a rule you will stick to.

Season one. You plant expecting about a hundred and fifty bushels an acre. Then the worst drought in decades settles on the Corn Belt. The harvest is a hundred and eighteen bushels. But because the whole Corn Belt is short, the price soars, from 5 dollars 79 at planting to 6 dollars 79 at harvest. If you sold your expected crop ahead, you now have to buy back corn you never grew, at the higher price, to fill your contract: a loss. If you sold nothing ahead, the high price makes up for the small crop, and you make money. Storing until June costs you, because the price drifts down.

Season two. Near-perfect weather: a hundred and seventy bushels an acre, far more than you expected, and the same everywhere else. So the price collapses, from 4 dollars 82 in April to 3 dollars 54 at harvest. Now the forward sale is the hero: every bushel sold in spring earned the spring price. Selling nothing ahead loses almost ninety dollars an acre. A record crop, and a loss: that is farming.

Season three. A slightly disappointing crop, a hundred and seventy-eight bushels, and a weak price in spring, 2 dollars 84, because a pandemic has closed the world's restaurants and ethanol plants. Then, after harvest, China begins buying American corn on a record scale and the price takes off, to 5 dollars 65 by the next June. Selling ahead was the worst choice of the six. Keeping the grain in a bin and waiting earned more than two hundred and seventy dollars an acre.

Add the three seasons together. Over these three years, selling nothing ahead and storing until June did best, about 191 dollars an acre. Selling everything ahead did worst. But change the three years and the ranking changes. What the game shows is that no rule wins every year. A forward sale takes away the risk of the price, but not the risk of the weather, and in a drought, a hedge on a crop you did not grow becomes a bet. That is why most American corn farmers also buy crop insurance that pays when their revenue falls, not just their yield. Notice too how small the numbers are. In two of the three years the farm barely covered its costs, whatever it did. The price is set somewhere else, by millions of farmers and the weather on several continents, and one farmer can only choose how to live with it.
Acre: Now look inside one acre of that farm, with the Department of Agriculture's own accounts for corn in 2025. An acre grew about 198 bushels, and at harvest a bushel sold for 3 dollars 93, so the crop was worth about 782 dollars. Then the bills. Fertilizer, mostly nitrogen, is the biggest operating cost, about 172 dollars an acre. Seed, much of it genetically engineered and patented, about 113. Then chemicals, repairs, hired services and fuel. Then the costs of what the farmer owns: the machinery wearing out, about 171 dollars an acre, and the land itself, valued at what it could be rented for, 190. Then the family's own work, taxes and overheads. Add it all up, and the acre cost about 901 dollars to grow. It lost 118.

So why plant at all? Follow the money in the order it is paid. The crop brings in 782 dollars. Seed, fertilizer and the other operating costs must be paid in cash, and leave 327. The machinery is already bought; its wear is real but it is paid for. The land is the farmer's own, or rented on a contract that runs for the year. And the farmer's own time is paid last, with whatever is left, which this year was less than nothing. A bushel needed 2 dollars 30 to cover the cash costs, and 4 dollars 55 to cover everything. It sold for 3 dollars 93. So the farmer plants: every acre covers its cash costs and pays something towards the machinery and the land. It is Part four's cost curve again. In the short run, a producer keeps going as long as the price beats the cost of the next unit. The land, the machines and the family's labour are what absorb the bad years.

And this is not a bad year. Here are thirty years of the same accounts for corn, soybeans and wheat. Count the bars below the line. By the Department of Agriculture's full accounting, corn failed to cover all its costs in 19 of 30 years, soybeans in 12, and wheat in 26 of 28. The good years are the spikes: 2008, 2011 to 2013, 2021 and 2022, when droughts, biofuel mandates or wars sent prices up. A loss in these accounts does not mean the farm goes bust. It means the land and the family's work earned less than they could have earned elsewhere: the farm survives by paying its owners less than the market rate. That is the first clue to this part's question.
Dollar: Chapter three. Where the food dollar goes.

Americans spent about 2.1 trillion dollars on food in 2025. Take one of those dollars and break it into a hundred cents. The Department of Agriculture's economists trace each cent back through the economy, to the industry whose work it pays for. The biggest slice by far, about a third, pays restaurants and cafes: the cooks, the waiters, the rent on the dining room. Then the food processors: millers, bakers, packers, canners. Then the shops that sell food, and the wholesalers behind them. Then a long tail: finance and insurance, trucks and warehouses, energy, advertising, lawyers and accountants. And the farms themselves? The work done on crop and livestock farms accounts for about 6 cents of the dollar. Less than advertising and energy put together, plus finance.

There is another way to count the farm's part: not the work done on farms, but the price farms are paid for the food we eat. By that measure, the farm share was 12.6 cents of the dollar in 2025. It depends a great deal on where you eat. Of a dollar spent in a grocery store, about 19 cents reached farms. Of a dollar spent in a restaurant, about 7.5: the rest pays for the kitchen and the service. Over time, the farm share moves with the price of crops. It rose in the price spikes of 2011 to 2014 and of 2022, and fell when prices fell. And as Americans spend more of their food money in restaurants, the overall share drifts down even if nothing else changes.

Here is the same arithmetic for one familiar thing: a loaf of white bread. According to Kansas's wheat commission, a sixty-pound bushel of wheat makes about 42 pounds of white flour, enough for about 70 one-pound loaves. In Sep 2026, wheat sold for about 6 dollars 72 a bushel on the world market, so the wheat in one loaf cost about 10 cents. The average loaf of white bread in an American shop cost 1 dollar 83. The wheat is about 5 percent of the price. Even when wheat spiked in 2022, after the invasion of Ukraine, it never reached 12 percent. The rest is milling, baking, packaging, trucking, the shop, and the brand on the bag. Double the price of wheat, and a loaf would cost you about ten cents more.
Treadmill: In 1958, the agricultural economist Willard Cochrane described what he called the treadmill. Here it is as a model. A hundred farms grow the same crop. A new method arrives, a better seed, say, that grows twelve percent more on the same costs. The first farmers to adopt it do very well. They grow more, and the price has not moved yet, because they are only a few. So their neighbours copy them, and output rises across the whole market. But people do not eat much more bread or corn because there is more of it, so to sell the extra, the price must fall, and fall a long way. By the time everyone has adopted, the price has fallen so far that the early adopters' extra profit is gone. And the farmers who never adopted are now losing money on every acre. They sell out to their neighbours, and farms get bigger and fewer. Then another new method arrives, and the treadmill turns again. The gains from all that ingenuity do not stay with farmers. They pass, through lower prices, to everyone who eats.

And here is the treadmill in America's records. For seventy years after the Civil War, an acre of American corn yielded about the same. Then, from the 1930s, came hybrid seed, then nitrogen fertilizer, bigger machines, genetically engineered seed and precision planting. Each hectare now yields about 7 times what it did before. But the price of a bushel, after inflation, has not risen in thirty years of booming demand, including the rise of corn ethanol; it has fallen. And the farms. In 1935 the United States had 6.8 million farms, averaging 155 acres. In 2025 it had 1.86 million, averaging 469. About the same land, worked by a fraction of the farms. Every new method made the survivors bigger and let everyone else go.
Inputs: Chapter five. Seed, fertilizer and machines.

Here is the shape of the business that surrounds the farm. In the middle, almost 1.9 million American farms. None of them can change the price of corn by growing more or less: each is far too small. Economists call that a price taker. On one side, the companies that sell to farmers. Seed and crop chemicals: Corteva, Bayer, which bought Monsanto, and Syngenta, owned by a Chinese state company. Fertilizer: Nutrien, CF Industries, Mosaic, Yara. Machinery: Deere, CNH, AGCO and Kubota. A handful of names in each. On the other side, the companies that buy from farmers: the grain traders, the meat packers, the food manufacturers. Again, a handful of names. The farmer buys from a few, and sells to a few, and is one of very many. That is the second clue.

Watch what the sellers have done with their side. In 1996, the seed for an acre of American corn cost about 27 dollars. In 2025, about 113: more than four times as much, as companies sold hybrids with patented genetic traits that resist insects and weed killers. Farmers paid it because the seed yields more. Fertilizer cost about 51 dollars an acre in 1996. In 2022 it reached 226, as the price of natural gas, from which nitrogen fertilizer is made, soared and the invasion of Ukraine disrupted supplies. Here is the other side of that bill. CF Industries, America's largest maker of nitrogen fertilizer, had revenue of about 4 billion dollars and a profit of 317 million in 2020. In 2022: revenue of 11 billion, and a profit of 3.3 billion, ten times as much. The farmer's worst year for costs was the fertilizer maker's best year ever.

Put the five years from 2021 to 2025 side by side, as profit kept from each dollar of sales. Growing corn, by the Department of Agriculture's accounts, kept about 3 cents on the dollar over those five years, and that includes the boom years of 2021 and 2022. The seed and chemical maker, Corteva, about 7. Mosaic, about 9. Deere, about 14, and CF Industries, about 22. The comparison is not perfectly fair, because the farm's accounts pay its owners a normal return on their land and labour before counting profit. But the pattern is the treadmill's: the farmer's gains are competed away, while the companies with patents, brands and scale keep theirs.
Traders: Follow a bushel of corn or soybeans after it leaves the farm. A truck takes it to a country elevator, a tall concrete store beside a railway or a river. From there it goes by train, or by barge, a few hundred thousand bushels to a string of barges, down the Mississippi. At export elevators on the river near New Orleans it is loaded onto ships, which carry it through the Panama Canal and across the Pacific, to feed mills that turn it into feed for pigs and chickens in China, Japan and Mexico. Almost every step of that journey, the elevators, the barges, the terminals and the contracts with the buyers abroad, belongs to a handful of trading companies.

Four companies dominate the world's grain trade, known in the business as the ABCD: ADM, Bunge, Cargill and Louis Dreyfus. They are among the largest companies on Earth by revenue. Cargill, privately owned by its founding families, took in about 154 billion dollars in the year to May 2025. ADM, about 80 billion in 2025. Bunge, about 70 billion, after it bought the Canadian trader Viterra. But look at what they keep. ADM's profit has averaged about 3 cents for every dollar of sales over the last ten years. A trader buys a bushel and sells it a few weeks later for almost the same price. It lives on volume, on the logistics it owns, and on the small differences in price between places, months and products.

Here is one of those differences. A soybean crusher, a business all four traders run, buys soybeans and presses them. By the exchange's standard reckoning, a sixty-pound bushel gives about forty-four pounds of meal, which feeds animals, and eleven pounds of oil, which goes into cooking and, increasingly, into diesel made from plants. The crusher's margin is what the meal and the oil sell for, less what the beans cost. On world prices, it has averaged about 30 dollars a tonne of beans since 1992, a few percent of the price. In 2026 it jumped to about 169 dollars, as American policies on biofuels pulled soybean oil into fuel tanks. Notice that the crusher does not care whether soybeans are dear or cheap. It cares about the gap. That is how a trader thinks, and why its margin is thin and steady while the farmer's swings.
Futures: Chapter seven. Selling a crop before it grows.

In the game, selling ahead meant a forward contract. The tool behind it is the futures market. A corn futures contract, traded in Chicago, is a promise to deliver 5,000 bushels in a given month, December say, at a price agreed today. In the spring the farmer sells contracts covering part of the crop. On the other side is someone who wants corn later at a known price, a feed mill or an ethanol plant, or a speculator who simply thinks the price will rise. Now the price falls through the summer, as it did in 2014. At harvest the farmer sells the real corn locally at the low price, and closes the contract with a gain of almost the same amount. The two cancel, and the farmer ends up with roughly the spring price. Gains and losses on the contract are paid every day, through the exchange, so neither side can walk away. What the farmer cannot remove is the gap between the local price and Chicago's, and the risk of having less corn than expected.

Here is the price that every one of those contracts is betting on, for thirty years. For a decade it hovered around two to three dollars a bushel. Then American law began to require ethanol in petrol, and a large share of the corn crop went to fuel. The drought of 2012 took it to a record. Record crops brought it back down for years. The pandemic, a Chinese buying spree and the invasion of Ukraine, one of the world's great grain exporters, sent it up again. Each spike lasted a year or two, because every farmer on Earth answers a high price the same way: by planting more.
Meat: Much of what farmers grow is never eaten by people directly. Most American corn that stays at home goes into animal feed or ethanol, and nearly all soybean meal is fed to animals. Cattle, hogs and chickens turn that grain into meat, eggs and milk, at a cost: an animal burns most of its feed simply to live and grow. Then the animals go to a packing plant, where they are slaughtered, cut and packed, and on to shops and restaurants. The packing plant is where this chain narrows.

Take beef. In 1980, the four largest beef packers bought about 36 percent of the young cattle fattened for slaughter in the United States. Today, about 85 percent, according to the Department of Agriculture. Four companies: Tyson, Brazil's JBS, Cargill, and National Beef. A cattle feeder in Kansas or Nebraska with animals ready for slaughter may have only two or three plants within trucking distance to sell to. Economists still argue about how much that costs cattle producers. But it means the farm's side of this market is many sellers facing very few buyers.

And yet the packers are not simply rich. Beef in American shops has never been dearer: a pound of ground beef cost about 1.48 dollars in 2000, and a record 6 dollars 92 in Aug 2026, as the national cattle herd shrank after years of drought and high costs. Ranchers selling cattle have had some of their best years. But look at Tyson, the biggest meat company in America. In 2021 and 2022 it kept about six cents of every dollar. Then its margins collapsed: chicken prices fell, and cattle became so scarce and expensive that beef stopped paying. In 2023 the whole company lost money. Since then it has kept about a cent on the dollar. Concentration gives the packers power over the price of cattle, but not over the number of cattle. When the animals run short, the squeeze runs the other way.
Brands: Chapter nine. From a bushel to a box.

Now line up the whole chain, from the field to the shop, by how much profit each kind of company keeps from a dollar of sales. Each bar is one company's average over the five years to 2025. On the left, the companies that sell to farmers: fertilizer, machinery, seed. Twenty, fourteen, nine, seven cents on the dollar. Then the farm, a few cents at most. Then the traders and the meat packers: two to four cents, Hormel's brands a little more. Then the brand owners, the makers of cereal, snacks and chocolate: ten to fifteen cents, except Kraft Heinz, about which more in a moment. And then the shops: two or three cents. It makes a smile. The money is kept at the two ends where something is hard to copy: a patent, a fertilizer plant, a brand that people ask for by name. In the middle, where the product is a commodity, a bushel, a carcass or a tonne of soybean meal, competition takes almost everything.

Two footnotes to the smile. A thin margin can still make a giant. Walmart, America's biggest grocer, sold about 675 billion dollars of goods in its latest year and kept about 3 cents of each dollar: still about 19 billion dollars of profit. Supermarkets live on turning their stock over quickly, many times a year. And a brand's power is not permanent. In 2025 Kraft Heinz, the maker of ketchup, cheese slices and macaroni, reported a loss of 5.8 billion dollars, mostly because it wrote down the value it puts on its brands and on the businesses it had bought, as its sales kept shrinking. A brand is a moat only as long as people keep asking for it.
State: Chapter ten. The state on the farm.

Every rich country pays its farmers, and the United States has done so since the Depression. In 1933 the New Deal began paying farmers to plant less, to lift prices that the treadmill and the slump had crushed. Since then, the payments have risen whenever prices fell. Around 2000, when crop prices were very low, government payments made up almost half of all farm income. The biggest year of all was 2020: payments to make up for China's retaliation against American soybeans in the trade war, and then pandemic relief, came to about 57 billion of today's dollars, again close to half of farm income. And the Department's forecast for 2026 is about 47 billion dollars, the second-largest on record. Why pay at all? Partly because farm income swings so violently, as you saw in the intermission. Partly because farmers, though few, are spread across many states, each with two senators. And partly because every government fears being unable to feed its people.

Governments also act on the other side: when food gets dear, they stop it leaving. India is the world's largest exporter of rice. On the twentieth of July 2023, to keep rice cheap and plentiful at home, it banned exports of ordinary white rice. The world price jumped, from about 492 dollars a tonne before the ban to 629 in Jan 2024, and importing countries in Africa and Asia paid more. In September and October 2024, with its own stores well stocked, India lifted the ban, and the price fell back, to about 466 dollars now. Every big farming country manages its food this way, with minimum prices, public stores, subsidies and trade rules. Food is the one market no government leaves alone.
Land: Chapter eleven. Land: who keeps the gain.

So where did the gains of a century of better farming go? Partly to everyone who eats. And partly into the land. Here is the value of all the farmland and farm buildings in the United States, after inflation. It rose through the 1970s boom, when farmers borrowed to buy more land at rising prices, and then collapsed, losing about half its real value by 1991, as interest rates soared and crop prices fell. Thousands of farms failed. Since then it has climbed almost without a break, to about 3.7 trillion dollars in 2026: about 4,122 dollars for every acre of American farmland, more than five times what an acre of corn earns in a good year.

This is the deepest clue to our question. The Department of Agriculture splits the yearly return on all farm assets in two. The gold part is the return from farming: what the crops and animals earn on the land and machines. Since 1990 it has averaged about 2.5 percent a year. The brown part is the return from the land itself becoming more valuable: about 4.6 percent a year. And the red is what happens when that reverses, as it did in the 1980s. For most of the last seventy years, American farmers have made more money from owning land than from farming it. They live poor, as the old saying goes, and die rich.

Why does the land capture the gains? Go back to our acre of corn. The crop brought in 782 dollars. Everything except the land cost about 710. So the most a farmer could pay for that acre this year, and still break even, was about 68 dollars. But land like it rents for about 190. The rent was set in better years, by farmers competing to farm more acres, and a bad year does not change it at once. The economist David Ricardo explained this two centuries ago: rent is what is left over after every other cost. When a new seed or a high price makes farming more profitable, farmers bid the gain into the rent and the price of land. When the price falls, whoever farms the land takes the loss. The landowner keeps the good years; the farmer lives through the bad ones.
Tropics: Chapter twelve. Cocoa, and the world's plate.

Some crops come from almost everywhere. Cocoa comes from one corner of one continent. In the 2022 to 2023 season, two neighbouring countries in West Africa, Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana, grew about 57 percent of the world's cocoa beans, almost all of it on small family farms of a few hectares each. The next season, bad weather and a spreading tree virus cut the crop, and the world's harvest fell by about 11 percent. Because chocolate eaters do not stop eating chocolate, the price did the rationing. Cocoa had cost about 2,369 dollars a tonne in 2022. By Jan 2025 it cost 10,710, more than four times as much. It has since fallen back to about 5,919.

Who paid? The chocolate makers, at first. Hershey kept about sixteen cents of each dollar for years; in 2025, about 8. Mondelez, the owner of Cadbury and Milka, fell to about 6. Then shoppers paid, as chocolate prices rose. And the farmers? In Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana, a state board sets the price paid to cocoa farmers for each season and sells much of the crop a year or more ahead. That protects farmers from crashes, but when the world price leapt, the price at the farm gate rose far more slowly. The boards' answer to a volatile price was the farmer's forward sale, made by the state.

Step back and look at the whole world's plate. The Food and Agriculture Organization adds up all the food each country produces and imports, less exports, waste and animal feed, and divides by its people. In 1961 the world had about 2,184 kilocalories of food a day for each person. In 2024, about 3,013, for a population more than two and a half times as large. China went from about 1,426, the years of the great famine, to 3,496. India from 2,064 to 2,717. Africa has gained least, and still has the least: that is where the next green revolution is needed. But the treadmill that made farming such a hard business made the world fed.
Landscape: Here is the landscape, as of November 2026. Each bubble is a company that files its accounts in the United States, placed by its revenue and by how much of each dollar it kept over five years. High and to the left, the input makers: CF Industries, Mosaic, Corteva, and Deere, the biggest of them. Low and to the right, the traders, ADM and Bunge, huge and thin. The meat companies, Tyson, Pilgrim's and Hormel, low as well. The brand owners, higher: PepsiCo, by far the largest, Mondelez, General Mills, Hershey, and Kraft Heinz pulled down by its write-downs. And Kroger, the largest supermarket chain that sells mostly food, with the thinnest margin of all. Many of the biggest players are not here at all, because they do not file in the United States: Cargill, the largest private company in America, Louis Dreyfus, China's COFCO, Bayer, Syngenta, Nestlé and Unilever.

And what to watch. Government payments: the Department of Agriculture forecasts about 47 billion dollars for 2026. The cattle herd: beef is at a record, and when ranchers start keeping heifers to rebuild their herds, prices and the packers' margins will turn. Biofuel rules, which now decide what soybean oil is worth. Cocoa, and whether West Africa's trees recover. Fertilizer, which follows the price of natural gas. And the farm share of the food dollar, which brings us to our call.
Called: Part ten's forecast to test is one of the most famous of the twentieth century. In 1968 the biologist Paul Ehrlich, the same man who would later lose the metals bet of Part nine, published The Population Bomb. It opened: the battle to feed all of humanity is over. It predicted that hundreds of millions of people would starve to death in the coming decades, whatever crash programmes were launched. India, it argued, could not feed itself. As the book went to press, Borlaug's dwarf wheat was already spreading across India and Pakistan. Here is the world's food supply per person: about 2,184 kilocalories a day in 1961, about 2,303 when the book appeared, and about 3,013 in 2024, for a population more than twice as large. Called it? No. Famines still came, in Bangladesh, in Ethiopia, in North Korea, mostly through war and misrule. But the mass starvation foretold did not come, because the farmers, the seed breeders and the fertilizer makers, the whole industry of this film, grew the food.

Now our own forecast, written down so you can check it. The farm share of an American food dollar was 12.6 cents in 2025. Since 2016 it has stayed between 12.0 and 14.3, rising when farm prices rise. In the first nine months of 2026, the world prices of maize, wheat, soybeans and beef all averaged more than a year earlier, by between five and eighteen percent. So our call: when the Department of Agriculture next publishes the food dollar, the farm share for 2026 will be higher than for 2025, comparing the two years in the same release, since the department revises its figures. We give it 70 percent. What could make us wrong: Americans moving still more of their food spending to restaurants, where the farm share is small, or margins further down the chain widening faster than farm prices. We will report the answer, right or wrong.
